---
title: "From linguistic records to probabilities"
---

A linguistic record does not determine its own statistical unit. An audio file may contain many word and vowel tokens; a vowel token may in turn contain a duration, a fundamental frequency, and a formant trajectory. Treating any one of these objects as a row produces a different dataset from the same record.

Before we count anything, we must specify the unit of observation and decide which differences among speakers, items, and tokens remain visible. The same issue arises with every kind of linguistic data. A corpus can be divided into documents, sentences, word tokens, or word types. A reading-time experiment can retain one row for each trial or average those trials by participant or sentence.

This module defines the observations, determines which comparisons answer a linguistic question, and then introduces probabilities over possible outcomes and events.

## Linguistic data and comparisons

First, we [turn linguistic records into data](linguistic-data.qmd). Once we distinguish a record from the observations extracted from it, we can state what each row represents, which columns identify it, and which speakers or words occur in more than one row.

Second, we [turn a research question into a comparison](making-sense-of-data.qmd). A numerical contrast is not interpretable until we know which response was measured, how the conditions differed, and whether participants and sentence items occurred in both conditions. These facts determine which difference we have estimated.

Third, we work through [Zipf's law](zipfs-law.qmd) by counting word tokens, grouping them into types, ordering the types by frequency, and comparing the observed counts with an inverse rank function. A rank frequency function may describe a corpus well, but that fit does not tell us which process produced the corpus.

## Probability

Now we can state the probability question. What results can the observation process produce, which groupings of those results matter, and how much probability should each grouping receive? A [sample space](possibilities-and-events.qmd) is the set of possible outcomes represented by the model. An [event](events.qmd) is a set of those outcomes. The outcome definition and the event definition must both follow from the linguistic record and the target comparison.

We do not always assign probabilities to every subset of the sample space. A [sigma-algebra](event-spaces.qmd) specifies which events are measurable. We construct generated event spaces from attested linguistic features, then define a [probability measure](probability-measures.qmd) that assigns a probability to each measurable event. The sample space, sigma-algebra, and probability measure form the probability space

$$
\langle\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}\rangle.
$$

Once the probability space is defined, we can calculate probabilities for relations among events. We begin with [mutually exclusive events](probability-concepts.qmd), whose intersection is empty, and introduce the standard comma notation for [joint probabilities](joint-probability-of-events.qmd). We then define [conditional probability](conditional-probability.qmd) by restricting probability to a conditioning event. The [chain rule](probability-factorization.qmd) follows by rearranging that definition, and [Bayes' rule](bayes-rule.qmd) follows by factoring the same joint probability in two orders. We conclude with [independence](independence.qmd): its conditional interpretation is invariance under conditioning, and its unrestricted definition is the product factorization.

The [chapter dependency graph](../learning-path.qmd) shows which later chapters use these definitions. The order matters: each page adds one object that the next page assumes. Begin by [deciding what one linguistic observation represents](linguistic-data.qmd).
